utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. We have some motions to deal with. The first one is on the request for exculpatory information, which I think is filed by counsel for Mr Delic on 1st April. I think Mr Moran will speak to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Your Honour, before that may I introduce a new member of our team today, who is going to speak for the prosecution on this issue. This is Mr Rod Dixon, who is an international law expert in the Office of the Prosecutor. He will take care of the arguments in this case. Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr Dixon is welcome to the team. Can we have appearances on this motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I am Eric Ostberg. I appear today with Mr Giuliano Turone, Ms. Teresa McHenry, Ms. Elles van Dusschoten and Mr. Rod Dixon, who I just introduced. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I know Mr. Moran is for this motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. May I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, you can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, judge. This is pretty straightforward stuff. In the opening statement Mr. Ostberg stood up and said he was going to prove that some or all of these people were prisoners of war under the Geneva Convention related to prisoners of war. Twice in written submissions to the Trial Chamber, in their pre-trial Memorandum and again in their response to pre-trial Memorandum filed in April the Prosecutor again said that they were going to make them prisoners of war under Geneva Convention 3 from 1949. Basically what I am asking for is evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor to negate that, to negate that these people are prisoners of war for purposes of the Geneva Convention 3, specifically Article 4 of Geneva Convention 3. That sets out basically six classes of people who are entitled to POW status. The first one is members of a regular armed force. There has been absolutely no evidence presented at this trial that would even lead one to be able to draw an inference on -- an inference that these people were members of somebody's regular armed force. The second group is militias, volunteer corps, organised resistance movements. There is some evidence that one can draw inference that those people -- some or all of these people were trying to form some sort of a partisan organisation or some sort of a resistance group. The third category is regular armed forces possessing an allegiance to a government that is not recognised by the detaining power. That is the Free French from World War II. There is no evidence of that. The fourth category is military contract or civilian aircrew, things like that. They do not meet that category. Fifth category is crews of merchant vessels. Again there is no evidence of that. Six is the levy en masse. I do not believe there has been any evidence these people can meet the criteria of a levy en masse for a very specific reason. These people, according to the Tadic Decision handed down last week and I believe in the Tadic appellate decision, are all citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The territory was Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do not think you can have a levy en masse in your own country. So that leaves category 2, which is the resistance partisan definition. They have to meet four requirements, the resistance organisation, not the individual people. The organisation that they are part of has to meet four criteria: they have to be commanded by a person responsible for their subordinates; that is command responsibility. That goes all the way back to The Hague Convention of, what, 1898. Secondly, they have to have a fixed, distinctive sign recognisable at a distance. Third, they have to carry their arms openly. Fourth, they have to conduct their operations in accordance with the laws and customs of war. That is straight out of the Geneva Convention. It is our position that if the prosecution maintains that these people are POWs for purposes of Geneva Convention 3, they have to prove these facts. They have got to get them into one of these categories. I do not think they can do it. They tell you they can. I think that the Rules are clear. If they have any evidence in their possession which negates any of those criteria, we are entitled to have it. I submit to you that the prosecution does have in its possession substantial evidence to show that the Bosnian Serb forces do not meet the requirements of Article 4 of the Geneva Convention, specifically Subsection 2 or for that matter subsection 6, which is the levy en masse as it goes to various categories of the definition, especially respecting laws and customs of war. I would submit that they cannot stand in front of this Tribunal with a straight face and say they do not have that evidence. In the Tadic Decision, which I quoted -- excuse me -- Blaskic decision, which I quoted in my Memorandum -- it is the decision on production of discovery materials from 27th January of this year -- the Tribunal set out a three-part test on whether or not exculpatory information should be turned over to the defence. The first question is whether the material is in the possession of the Prosecutor. Again, I think that, given the indictments that have been handed down in other cases, they cannot conceivably argue that there is not evidence in the possession of the Prosecutor to negate at least one of the elements of the definition of prisoner of war as it would conceivably apply to the people held in the Celebici camp. The second thing is -- second part of the test is whether the materials contain exculpatory evidence. I submit to the Tribunal that evidence that the Serb partisans as a group did not follow the laws and customs of war would be exculpatory in that it would negate part of the definition of prisoner of war in Article 4(2) of the Geneva Convention on prisoners of war. The third prong of the test is whether the Prosecutor believes that the exculpatory evidence is protected by Rule 66C. Rule 66C is, of course, the confidentiality Rule. That is something that the Prosecutor would have to plead and prove, that it would prejudice further investigations or it may be contrary to the public interest or the security interest. If they rely on Rule 66C, they have to provide the information to the Trial Chamber for in camera inspection. I think it is pretty straightforward stuff. I believe they have exculpatory information to negate allegations that they have made orally and in writing to the Trial Chamber. I want it. I want to look at it. I want to be able to present it to the Trial Chamber, if it becomes necessary. That is the long and the short of our motion for exculpatory evidence, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You are sure they have such documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if they do not have evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because you have not directed attention to any particular exculpatory matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the prosecution does not have evidence that the Bosnian Serbs were violating the laws and customs of war, the indictment that has been returned and the Rule 61 on Karadzik is based on no evidence and just run down the list of indictees. I submit to the Trial Chamber that when the prosecution sends an indictment over to the Trial Chamber or to a judge of the court or the Tribunal for confirmation, that they have evidence to support their allegations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: But you should know what evidence you are seeking. You should not merely be fishing. It should not be a roving one. You should know exactly what they should turn over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think they should turn over to me all the evidence they have which shows that the Bosnian Serbs, partisans, did not follow the laws and customs of war, that they did not bear arms openly, that they did not have a commander responsible for his subordinates, that they did not have a fixed, distinctive sign recognisable at a distance. I have laid out what I believe they have in my written submission to the Trial Chamber, and I submit -- I have not been through their files. I do not know what is there. I believe that the prosecution is acting in good faith in other cases, where they return indictments. Mr. Ostberg stood in front of the Trial Chamber on the first day of this trial in his opening statement and said he is going to make them POWs. I do not think he can but he says he is going to do it. The prosecution said in their pre-trial Memorandum filed back in February or March they were going to make some or all of these people prisoners of war. I do not think they can do it. They said in their response to the pre-trial Memorandum which was filed about five weeks in the trial, they said it again. Yes, your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: In fact, the agreed witness of fact who appeared before us, will you be cross-examining him about his status at the time when he was taken to Celebici camp? .

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: They all claim they were innocent citizens who were nothing to do with the conflict and they were without any reason detained in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I think you are doing very well in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, judge. I appreciate that, but again I am not the one that made these allegations. I am not the one who has made the submission three times to the Trial Chamber that they can do it. If the Trial Chamber recalls, in my pre-trial Memorandum I told you I did not think they could. They came back after that was filed, after they had a chance to read it and said they could and they would. Well, if they are going to try it, if they think they can, if they are telling you in good faith they are going to do it, I am entitled to the exculpatory information to show these people were not POWs. That is what I am asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear the defence of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honours. The prosecution response to the defence's version and these submissions is that this request should be denied for two main reasons. Firstly, all evidence and information, including exculpatory evidence, has been handed to the defence by the Prosecutor's Office concerning the Bosnian Serb forces that were operating in the Konjic municipality, including those who were operating in and around the Celebici area specifically. It is for the Prosecutor to, on the basis of this evidence, prove that the requirements of the Geneva Conventions and Article 2 have been met and to make the necessary legal arguments in the course of this trial. We do not believe that this is a matter which is the subject of this motion which specifically requests exculpatory evidence. Secondly, evidence and information relating to other armed forces is totally irrelevant to the present case. The defence have made no prima facie showing that it is relevant to the present case, to the guilt of the accused in this case, and it would be unreasonable in the circumstances for the Prosecutor to have to make this kind of information available to the defence. The defence have stated that there are four requirements that must be met for the armed force to be a lawful armed force so that those persons who may have been part of this armed force who were then detained in the Celebici camp would be protected under Article 2 of the Statute. The first one is that they must be commanded by a person responsible for subordinates; the second is that they must have a fixed, distinctive sign recognisable at a distance; the third is that they must carry arms openly; and the fourth is that they must conduct the operations in accordance with the laws and customs of war. The defence is essentially requesting this evidence if it negates any of these requirements on the basis that if any of these requirements are not established then Mr. Delic's guilt will be negated in terms of the Article 2 charges of the statute. The Prosecutor submits that we have given to the defence all evidence and information, including exculpatory evidence concerning the armed forces, that certain persons in the Celebici camp might have been part of. It is evident from this information that these were irregular armed forces that were operating in part of the Konjic municipality, which were broadly linked to the regular armies of the Bosnian Serb Army, the VRS, and the JNA, which later became the Yugoslav Army. We have no further evidence or information in our possession or under our control concerning the armed forces that were operating in the Konjic municipality. We have handed everything to the defence under our disclosure obligations under Rule 66A. We have gone further than that and upon request under Rule 66B we have handed all documents and objects material to the preparation of the defence and which the Prosecutor will rely on as evidence, or which were obtained from the accused, and we have fulfilled all our obligations under Rule 68. We have handed over all material under that Rule in relation to the armed forces that were operating in the Konjic municipality. The defence have not in their written submissions or in their oral submissions today made any prima facie showing that the Prosecutor has any further evidence concerning the Bosnian Serb armed forces which were operating in the Konjic municipality in our possession or control at the moment. If the defence is requesting information about other irregular armed forces operating in other parts outside of the Konjic municipality of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or about the Bosnian Serb Army itself, the VRS, or the JNA or VJ, we submit that such information is totally irrelevant to the present case. It in no way concerns the guilt of the accused under Article 2 of the Statute, and it is our submission that the defence have not shown that such evidence would be relevant to the guilt of the accused in this case. It is irrelevant in respect of the VRS, the JNA and the VJ because these are regular armies. They are widely acknowledged to be organised armies, with command structures, with uniformed troops, which carry arms openly, and even if they did commit violations of the laws and customs of war, which we do not dispute as the Office of the Prosecutor, this in no way would justify persons in those armies losing their prisoner of war status. The Geneva Conventions are quite explicit on this point, that you retain your prisoner of war status, even if you yourself commit violations or other people commit violations if you are part of a regular army. Secondly, in relation to information about other irregular forces, this information is also totally irrelevant to the guilt of the accused. We, as the Prosecutor, are only required to show, we would submit, that the irregular forces that the victims in the Celebici camp might have been part of were forces that met the requirements of the Geneva Conventions. We do not have to show that all forces operating in other areas that might have been irregular forces, that the victims had nothing to do with, met the requirements of the Geneva Conventions, only those irregular forces within the municipality of Konjic that the victims may have been part of in this particular case. The defence have not demonstrated why any other information is required, why it either affects the guilt of the accused or the credibility of the prosecution evidence, which are the requirements of Rule 68. It would also be unreasonable, we would submit, to expect the defence to have access to all the Prosecutor's evidence in other cases and investigations concerning any Bosnian Serb perpetrators, or Bosnian Serb forces, or the Bosnian Serb Army, or the regular Serb Army throughout the whole of the territory of the former Yugoslavia from 1991 onwards, especially when there is no clear purpose for receiving this information and we are not obliged to do so, as we have argued under the Rules. The Prosecutor quite plainly fails to see the point of the defence's request in this regard, and would therefore request that it should be denied. Just two final points before concluding, your Honours. Firstly, it should be pointed out that certain of the requirements which the defence mentioned for armed forces to qualify as legal armed forces in terms of the Geneva Conventions have, in fact, been modified over time by international humanitarian law, particularly in terms of the additional protocols which came later in 1977. It is no longer necessary to display a distinctive sign. It is also no longer necessary to carry your arms openly in all circumstances and, as I have mentioned before, if you commit violations of the laws and customs of war, this does not mean that you lose your status as a prisoner of war, whether you are in a regular or an irregular army. Of course, you can be punished for these violations, but you do not lose your protection to be treated humanely and not to have grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions committed against you. Moreover, in terms of Article 2, in the present case Article 2 is, in fact, we would submit, applicable even if the persons were not prisoners of war. So, even if the persons who the Prosecutor might argue qualify as prisoners of war do not for some reason qualify, so we fail to meet the requirements, then they are still protected as civilians, and indeed we have submitted that many people are purely protected as civilians. But even if we attempted to show that some were prisoners of war and then they did not end up being prisoners of war, they are still protected as civilians. The point of this is: even if we had some information, arguably, that showed that the victims were not prisoners of war, they would still be protected as civilians under Article 2 of the Statute. So in conclusion, your Honours, we submit that the request should be denied, firstly because we have complied with all of our obligations concerning the forces in the Konjic municipality, and, secondly, because any other information is totally irrelevant to the guilt of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: May I say something? Under Rule 68 the obligation of the Prosecutor is limited to the evidence which is known to him. I think in this regard Mr. Ostberg's statement that is all the exculpatory evidence which is known to him should be sufficient unless you can show that that statement is not correct. Ordinarily it is the Prosecutor who can say what is known to him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that the prosecution is drawing a very narrow and unrealistically narrow definition of what is exculpatory and let me explain why I believe this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: I am putting the emphasis on the words "known to him". He cannot supply to you what is not known to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: It is not what is known to Mr. Ostberg is the test. The test is what is known to the Office of the Prosecutor. Let us start with that. The question then becomes what is relevant, what is exculpatory. Even reading the Prosecutor's response to my motion, I think we can both agree that you do not look at this person to decide whether or not this person is a prisoner of war under Geneva Convention 3. What you look at is the larger picture, so that, for instance, if I am a member of a partisan organisation that commits war crimes on a regular basis, even if I do not commit war crimes, I am not entitled to POW status. I may have some other kind of status, but I am not entitled to prisoner of war status. Given Dr Calic's testimony about the All People's Defence, which, as I recall, was testimony that the Central Government in the former Yugoslavia set up this military organisation throughout the country, basically to carry on partisan war in case someone invaded, you are looking at more than just in the Konjic area; you are looking at a larger picture for the organisation that these people were members of. If, for instance, they have evidence that the SDS, the Bosnian Serb political party, was arming, controlling, dealing with these partisan groups, these irregular groups, then it is part of that larger picture, and the question is not whether Partisan Smith, who lived in Bradina, was following the laws and customs of war; it is did the organisation as a group follow the laws and customs of war? Again, I do not think -- in fact, given the two Tadic decisions, the Appellate Chamber Decision and the Decision from the Trial Chamber last week, the Judgment and Opinion on that, I do not know how they can meet any of these requirements of putting these people -- making these people protected persons under Article 2 of the Statute or anywhere in the Geneva Conventions. They say they can. Maybe they have got evidence out there that they can do it. If they think they can, it is exculpatory for my client, exculpatory evidence to be able to show that these people did not have prisoner of war status. Again I am not the person who made the allegation that some or all of these people were prisoners of war. Quite the contrary. From Day 1, in the very first written submission I made to this Trial Chamber, I said I did not think that they could do it. I am taking the prosecution at its word that they have proof that these people were prisoners of war, that Mr. Ostberg and the Prosecution in their written submissions, their oral submissions to the Trial Chamber were acting in good faith, and taking their own pleadings -- their response to my motion about looking at the larger picture, I want the evidence of that larger picture to show that these people were not prisoners of war. The other easy solution is they can stand up right now and stipulate they were not prisoners of war and I will sit down and I am a happy person. They cannot have it both ways, judge. They cannot have their cake and eat it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do I understand your argument is by way of deduction now because they say these persons are prisoners of war, and that material is what you rely on as exculpatory and you want it to be turned over to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I am relying upon is this: the prosecution has made certain factual and legal representations to the Trial Chamber. I guess you can say that is deduction. I would not stand here and tell you that Mr. Ostberg and the rest of the prosecution team, or for that matter the Office of the Prosecutor in general, was not acting in good faith when they made those factual and legal representations to the Trial Chamber. I am presuming that they are going to be able to do it. As Judge Jan pointed out, they have not done it yet, but they tell me that they are going to, they tell you that they are going to. I think we have to take them at their word. As you walk out the first floor of this building, as you walk out those double doors, right next to it by the Press Office there is a group of hand-outs and it has most of the indictments that have been presented by the Trial Chamber. Anybody can walk by and just grab them and take a look at them -- excuse me -- indictments presented by the Office of the Prosecutor; the Trial Chamber obviously does not present them. They are making the allegations both to this Trial Chamber and the other Trial Chamber that there were systematic violations of the laws and customs of war by Bosnian Serbs, the people that I say are part of this larger organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually my real anxiety is I am still what I would call in the wilderness about the arguments, because, if your contention is correct, you are assuming that they have exculpatory material which you should have, and therefore they should turn them over to you, but the ideal is that you should point out such exculpatory materials which you think they have, not necessarily they knowing what you think is exculpatory material. You should tell them what those materials are which you know they have, which they ought to turn over to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I do not have access to their files, I cannot tell you what they have got that they ought to give me. What I am saying is there are classes of information that they say they have, either directly or indirectly, by sending indictments over to be confirmed by various members of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: You really do not know those materials. You think there are materials or there are likely to be materials which are exculpatory of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Again, your Honour, if the prosecution would let me spend a couple of days reading through their files, I am sure I could tell you exactly what they have got that I want, but I do not think that that is -- that is not very likely to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: This is my main problem, because if you really know what those materials are, let them deny it that they do not have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I want everything that they have got to show that Bosnian Serb irregulars did not meet the criteria of Article 4, the definition of prisoner of war, or, in the alternative, as I say, I would be just as happy as I could be if Mr. Ostberg stands up and stipulates that these people were not prisoners of war. Either one makes me happy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Because when I read your motion, I just myself did not even know what to think about it. I was thinking about everything possible in the argument as a whole, everything which they have which leads to the determination whether these people are prisoners of war or not. There might be a mass of materials. That is a very difficult thing. That is not a prima facie argument as to what you want from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Well, first, I would ask the Trial Chamber to take judicial notice of the records of the Tribunal in each indictment and the confirmation of each indictment. Let us start with that. That has been returned. They put me between a rock and a hard place, that I cannot tell you exactly what they have got. All I can tell you is they have made representations to the Tribunal that they have evidence, that these people did not follow the laws and customs of war. I want that portion of that evidence that they tell the Tribunal they have got, not what they have told me they have, that shows the larger organisation that Dr Calic talked about and that these people do not meet the requirements for prisoners of war under the Geneva Conventions. They have got it, they have got the investigators, they have got the access to Interpol, they have got the access to the FBI, various governmental organisations. I do not have that. They have got it. They have got it in their files. You know they have got it in their files. I know they have got it in their files. Mr. Ostberg knows they have got it in their files. Or in the alternative --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: There are two aspects of the questions you are raising: first, what is known and, second, what you should try to come and find out. I think their obligation is limited to what is known to them. Whether they are prisoners of war or not is a question of interpretation of the evidence. You have been cross-examining the witnesses to find out their status. So when we have the entire evidence, we will know whether they were prisoners of war or not. That is a matter that can be taken up at the end of the trial when the argument starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are doing very well in asking about their status.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, judge. Again, I do not want to get into a situation somewhere down the road where somebody says: "So and so was a commander and we all wore uniforms that had insignia on them. They carried our AK47s for the whole world to see, and I saluted as I walked by the Commander." I do not want to have that pop up and then be coming back to the Trial Chamber asking for a six or eight-week continuance, adjournment, trying to get that information that I am asking for. Again I think that the Prosecutor is drawing an awfully narrow view. I do not want to say they are talking out of both sides of their face, but it is coming close. Either they have got evidence people are prisoners of war or they do not. If they do not, then they do not and they ought to tell us all that. If they do, then, if they have evidence showing that the organisation as a group, the larger organisation -- they are trying to narrow this down to the Konjic area. You can read in their proceedings that you look at the larger organisation. Then you can re-read Dr Calic's report talking about how the whole country was set up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Dr Calic was merely giving an opinion, but where you have witnesses, some of them have admitted they were members of the SDS and others have not. They all claimed they were civilians and had nothing to do with the conflict and yet they were taken without any reason to the Celebici camp and detained there. This is the evidence we have so far got.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. I agree. I agree with you totally that there is absolutely no evidence before this Trial Chamber that these people are prisoners of war under the Geneva Convention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is a question of interpretation, whether they have their status or not in the camp. We can decide on that only after the entire evidence has been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I understand that. At least in my opinion there is zero evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: You are quite right to make any contention in support of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Given that, the Office of the Prosecutor keeps coming back to this Trial Chamber in writing and oral submissions that they are going to prove it. They say they have got evidence of it. They are making the contention. I think it would be a whole lot easier if Mr. Ostberg just stood up right now and said: "These people were not prisoners of war under Geneva Convention 3." If he said that, I will withdraw the motion. I am a happy man and we can go about the rest of our lives and finish this trial --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Which year, judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Before Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Which Christmas, judge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: 1997 Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: My wife and child will appreciate that, if I am home for Christmas. If they want to do that, that is fine with me. I think they have put themselves on the horns of a dilemma. They have made a legal allegation. They have made a factual allegation. They have made allegations to this Trial Chamber. I am basically saying: "Put up or shut up. I want evidence that you have got that shows that you are not -- that you cannot make your case." If they want to stand up right now and stipulate that nobody in the Celebici camp met the criteria of being a prisoner of war under the Geneva Convention related to prisoners of war, that ends the matter, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually, why are they here if they come up to say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I do not know, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: That is why they have not said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I do not know if they have any evidence or we have got anything anywhere or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: The matter is still open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is true, judge, but as an open matter I do not want to have to be asking for a massive adjournment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I see your point. You keep pursuing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We will deliver a Ruling later. It is not a Ruling we can just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Now the next motion is the one still by Mr. Moran on the designated expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Actually I think that is an objection and I want to apologise. I have notice that the cover left a word out. That was read about 12 times. It just goes to prove that big type is easy to misplace things on. Again I think this is pretty straightforward stuff. On January 25 the Trial Chamber issued an Order which is attached to my objection. What it says is: if you have an expert witness, you have to do certain things. You have to do it by a certain time. If you do not meet the deadline, then you can apply to the Trial Chamber for good cause shown. I have got a motion wandering around some place asking to designate an expert witness out of time on Bosnian nationality. That did not appear that it was going to be an issue in the case. When it became an issue in the case, I asked for an expert witness. We do not have any objection to this witness testifying right now about what he saw, so long as the testimony is limited to what anyone could see without special training and without special experience. The problem is: from the materials that were given to us about this witness, it appears that he is going to be testifying to some great extent on things like -- I have forgotten -- has his profession been identified publicly?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Okay. Things like medical diagnoses. Now that requires special expertise. In fact, I think we can all agree that medicine is as much an art as it is a science and that a diagnosis of whatever it is relies to some great extent not only on the training and experience but also on opinion, and that goes right to the heart of what is an expert witness. The hypothetical I used in my objection was this: in America in traffic accident cases we often have engineers who are accident reconstruction people. They are expert witnesses who can take -- the example I used is skid marks -- they can measure skid marks and estimate within a fairly narrow parameter how fast the car was going when it hit the brakes, just based on the length of the skid marks. Now it is not expert testimony or opinion testimony, I do not believe, to say that the skid marks are 57.5 metres long. That is something that anybody can go out with a tape measure and measure, but to say that in turn based on that the vehicle that made those skid marks was going -- pick a number -- 47 kms an hour, that becomes expert testimony. So the heart of my objection is this: if this witness wants to come in and testify to the same kinds of facts that I could testify to or that anyone out in the audience could testify to -- another example in my motion is the emergency room physician who says: "The guy came in covered with blood." Anybody can testify to that. That requires no expertise, no training, no experience, no opinion. Then when you go much beyond that on why this person was covered with blood, then you start getting into the areas of expert witnesses, opinion, diagnosis, things like that. So I am not objecting to him getting on the stand and saying: "A man came in and he looked skinny." I object to testimony about diagnosis, and their written submissions -- it appears to be diagnoses -- half of it is in Latin -- all through this stuff. So if the Trial Chamber is clear on the distinction I am drawing between expert testimony and non-expert testimony -- I would like to have this guy's resume. I designated an expert witness who is a physician actually on the deadline date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: For how long did you have a copy just of his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Judge, what we have is -- and there is some dispute about that and we talked about it yesterday -- there was some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: The English version was probably not delivered to you earlier but you had his testimony in Serbo-Croat for a long time now but you are raising an objection now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. For an expert witness there are other things you want to do. I will give an example from this case. The minute that Dr Calic was designated as an expert witness, we ran her through a bunch of computers to find out what she had written so we would be prepared to cross-examine her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is not entirely an expert witness. What he saw is a question of fact. What he observed is a question of fact. Then he gives his opinion. You have had his testimony for a long time. Now you are objecting that he should not be examined as an expert witness. He was also a witness to the fact, as you admitted, because what he saw on the body of a particular person is a question of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: There is no question about it, judge. If he says there was a scar on my left leg, that is a fact question. If there is a scar on my left leg, you can see it, I can see it, anybody out in the audience can see it and testify to it. That is not expert testimony. I am happy to have him testify to that. I have no objection to that, but the minute he says that that scar was caused --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: That is a purely technical point. He is a witness and you have got the gist of his testimony. Now to say he should not be examined as an expert, I do not think that is on really. That is my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Of course you know I respect your personal opinion on that. I am making my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: He is a witness all right. You have got the gist of his testimony for a long time now with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: So, judge, like I say, our objection is not -- again if you draw the distinction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually you really do not want him to testify as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. I want him to testify as a fact witness, just like I would testify, if heaven forbid that were to occur, or anyone in the building would testify. As long as he does not get into opinions and things involving special expertise, then he is not an expert witness, he is a fact witness. He has been properly designated as a fact witness, and we can go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: So if he gives his opinion about a particular situation, you think it should not be relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, and especially having looked at the list of people that was given, I think that maybe three of them have been designated -- there is like a bunch of people. About 30 names are in this packet we were given. As I went through them last night, I believe four of them are witnesses in this case. I did not frankly go through and see which ones are mentioned in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Does your client suffer any prejudice if he testifies as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: The prejudice would be this: I do not know what this man has published in the past; I do not know what his training is. On the expert physician that I designated, I provided everybody with his training experience, everything he has ever published in his whole life and if when Dr Prince, my expert, gets on the witness stand, if he ever does, and begins to testify, the prosecution is going to be able to reach down into their briefcases and come up with the 100 or 110 published articles from Dr Prince and woe betide Dr Prince if he testifies differently than he published. Those are the kind of things that separate experts from non-experts. I have published several Law Review articles. If I were to get up in front of a court and argue a position inconsistent with what I had published some place else, I am sure that the lawyer on the other side, if he was any good, would have copies of those articles to hand to the trial court and say: "What's going on?" It is the same concept, judge. With that ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Do I understand that to mean that you are not properly equipped to cross-examine him as an expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, that comes to the heart of it. I do not know what this man's training experience was. I have not seen his resume, his curriculum vitae, which the Trial Chamber says I am entitled to. That would include things like what he has published. If he has published an article on -- I believe he is a surgeon. If he has published an article on that, I want to be able to know about that. The other thing is this: it appears from the written documents that I have seen that there were a lot of things that were done in these physical examinations, things like X-rays were taken, laboratory tests were done, that type of thing. Well, I am not that kind of doctor, and I do not know whether your basic surgeon can interpret an old X-ray or an X-ray to show there was an old injury there. I just flat don't know, but if this guy is a radiologist, I would like to know that. If he has training in radiology, I would like to know that. If he has training in psychiatry because he talked to half a dozen or a dozen of these witnesses, sending them off to see psychiatrists, I think that is highly relevant. Depending on what the diagnoses was on these people that he sent off to see psychiatrists, a couple of them are witnesses. If they have big time psychiatric problems, that goes directly to their ability to be a competent witness. I do not know all of that. I would sure like to. I am going to learn a lot of it on cross. All of these things go to the weight to be given to the testimony. Like I say, I do not know -- he may very well have published something in Paris.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us hear it. Let us have his testimony and you can ask him all these things in cross-examination. Then we will know what weight is to be placed on his testimony. It is premature at this stage to say that he should not be examined at all. Partly his testimony is of an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: First, your Honour, again I have never said he is not to be examined at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Let us examine him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If my objection is overruled, that is no problem. I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: We still have to hear why they have put him forward as an expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: If he has to give such a testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: He has -- firstly, for the knowledge of the defence of what is going on in this case of this witness, the statements made by him was given to them, as I stated yesterday, during the last summer, and they have had all possibilities to see what it is all about. On our witness list which we presented to the court in due time, as we were asked to do, his name was on it as number 12 and the text which we gave to the defence was the following: "Physician. He visited and issued medical certificates on a number of former detainees of Celebici camp." That has been known to the defence since this list landed with them. We did not put him on the list as an expert, but we gave notice very clearly of what he is going to testify about. He would be, in my civil law system, a mixed witness. We separate in the civil law system, between experts being appointed by the court. All others who are pure fact witness or mixed witness are treated like witnesses. That might have had some reflection on the way in which I put him on this witness list. I think it is not clear to me that this contention made by Mr. Moran from the point of view of American law is correct. In my submission this is not and it does not draw a distinction between factual observation and opinion. You always land sometimes with witnesses who have expertise and have seen things belonging to the fact. As I said in my -- I am quite used to that in my system and they are always put forward as witnesses. I think we come down to again a pure matter of admissibility on this witness. We know what he is going to testify to and we have to ask the question again: is what he is going to tell us relevant? Has it a probative value? I think we would answer "yes" to both these questions. Then we would ask the last question again: if it is outweighed to secure a fair trial. I think this is not prejudicial at all to the defence or the accused to have this person giving evidence of what he saw on people who had been detained in the Celebici camp. I think I have explained why I did not put him on the list as a fact -- as an expert witness. He is in my opinion something of a mixture and he falls in the general witness category. I ask your Honour's permission to bring him as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ostberg, is there any requirement in our Rules that an expert witness should be specifically mentioned as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: No. I cannot say that. There are Rules on witnesses and I am not aware of something like that. So I feel very confident when I put him on the list in the way we did. Thank you, your Honours. I do not think I have more to add.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Just one quick thing. Judge Jan, you asked a question about anything in the Rules. The Trial Chamber on January 25th entered an order -- entered a decision. Paragraph 1 says: "The prosecution or the defence for each accused will provide the other party with timely notice of potential expert witnesses. The notice will include the name of the witness, the witness' CV and a statement of the areas about which the witness will testify". Then this Trial Chamber went on to set out deadlines. If there is no longer a need to designate expert witnesses, that is fine with me. I have no problem with that. In the Delalic case this Trial Chamber in a Decision of the motion of the prosecutors to allow investigators to follow the trial issued on 27th March -- this Trial Chamber said: "An expert witness is one specifically skilled in the field of knowledge about which he is required to testify. The question of whether a person is an expert is one of law for the determination of the Trial Chamber." I think that the Trial Chamber is going to have to decide: does he meet the first sentence of your decision of March 27th, or again I have no objection if the Trial Chamber wishes to rescind the order of January 25th, 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I do not know about that. I think it depends on the status under which he testifies. If he is not testifying as an expert, it does not have to comply with those conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Definitely if his testimony includes his expertise, definitely it has to comply with those provisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: I agree with that wholeheartedly and I think I have set that out in my written submission. There may be a question about what is an expert but that is a question of law for the Trial Chamber. I have set out what I think the law is. Mr. Ostberg has set out what he thinks the law is on what is an expert. I do not think that an expert witness is someone who is just appointed by the court. If that were true, then there would not be any need for me to designate experts. An expert is somebody who has got special skilled training.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Giving his opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And is basing it either on his skill, opinion or training. That is correct, judge. No question about it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have a proposal. I am not sure my colleagues will agree with me, but I will seek their agreement as I speak. I think the way to cut through this difficult problem is for us to go ahead and bring the witness to the witness stand and let the prosecution go ahead and examine him, with this understanding, that the prosecution will as soon as possible, and I hope that should be either through the next break or by the lunch break at least, supply us with his CV, his curriculum vitae for us to examine. If appears at the end of the examination and cross-examination that we would require additional cross-examination based on his curriculum vitae and if he has given opinions that we want to enquire into further that we have not been able to prepare for, then the prosecution could either agree to bring him back a week from now for additional cross-examination or keep him here for a week for additional cross-examination, or whatever would be appropriate under the circumstances, but I think the concern we are all having is that if he gets into an area of expertise, we have no knowledge about his background, training, things of that nature, which might be quite relevant to his ability to give the opinions that he will seek to give. Those are the things that concern us, and I hope that that proposal is acceptable. I think it makes sense for all of us to pursue it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: I am not sure that I can provide the defence or the Trial Chamber with his CV. I am not in possession of it. The first question when he is put on the stand would be to ask him on his education, his university training, his speciality, etc, etc. I happen to know that he is a specialist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I suppose that should be acceptable to you for the time being. Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only speak for myself, but I think that probably is acceptable, if we can develop all that information from the witness stand, but with the understanding that if we develop information that would require us to prepare for additional cross-examination of this witness, that the prosecution would make him available within a reasonable amount of time, a few days, a week, something of that nature; otherwise it is of no use to go through that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JAN
utterances.text: Yes, you should, because you have not given the defence his background.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Okay. I quite agree. I accept this way of handling it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the nature of the opinion you expect of him will determine whether he could go forward to have that exercise, because if you want him to give expert opinions of really an erudite nature, you expect him to testify to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: And bring him back at a later point in time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: I think this should conclude this matter, because the objection has been overcome. We will take it as that. The Trial Chamber will now rise and reassemble at 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI WHYTE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostberg?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: During the break something has come up that forces me to ask for an immediate closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTBERG
utterances.text: Pages 2850 - 2858 in closed session (12.20 pm. - Hearing adjourned until 10.00 tomorrow morning
